terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive (an inchoative: “begin to be old”)
evidence: Cic. Sen. 38: ita sēnsim sine sēnsū aetās senēscit
terms.comment: Of people, and of things that wane, like the moon or the day.

terms.gloss: be up in years, be getting on
terms.grammar: participle of prōvehō with the ablative aetāte, agreeing with the person
evidence: Cic. Sen. 4.10: nōn admodum grandem nātū, sed tamen jam aetāte prōvectum (Lewis & Short s.v. prōvehō)
terms.comment: Literally “carried forward in age”: no longer young, though not yet very old, as Cicero's example shows.

phrases.latin: ita sēnsim sine sēnsū aetās senēscit nec subitō frangitur, sed diūturnitāte exstinguitur
phrases.english: so life grows old little by little, unnoticed; it doesn’t snap, it slowly fades out

phrases.latin: tempora lābuntur, tacitīsque senēscimus annīs, et fugiunt frēnō nōn remorante diēs
phrases.english: time glides by; we grow old with the silent years, and the days run off with no bridle to hold them

sources: Lewis & Short: senesco · Lewis & Short: proveho
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 76–77, 324.
